extracted.intended_audience: funders, grant peer reviewers (chairs & committee members), research administrators and policy-makers interested in grant peer review quality
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for conducting and improving grant peer review processes, drawn from qualitative interviews with CIHR Project Grant Competition reviewers, Chairs and Scientific Officers. Focuses on threats to integrity (training, scoring, bias) and suggested procedural/practice remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of training and limited opportunities to learn
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants reported informal or no training for reviewer/Chair/Scientific Officer roles; reviewers described a 'learn as you go' model and often relied on mentors or personal experience rather than formal instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide comprehensive, standardised training on reviewing and scoring (including scoring calibration), make reviewer training accessible (consider mandatory inclusion in PhD/postdoc curricula), offer reviewer training conferences/workshops, and ensure training is feasible given reviewers' time constraints. Note: CIHR provided written guides but participants often did not read or consider them sufficient as training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenges in differentiating and rating applications of similar strength (the 'meritorious middle')
rubrics_metrics.description: Committee members struggled to reliably distinguish and score many fundable applications clustered in the middle of the distribution; participants referred to a 'mushy middle' where there was no clear scientific 'fatal flaw' to separate grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop clearer guidelines for assessing mid-range applications, consider procedural changes (eg, ranking instead of fine-grained rating), encourage calibration discussions to set floor/ceiling examples, and ensure verbal descriptions of scores accurately reflect funding intent. Acknowledge that interest or topic 'fashionability' can inappropriately influence differentiation and counter this with explicit criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers weighting reputations and relationships in the review process
rubrics_metrics.description: When unclear how to rate grants, reviewers reported relying on applicant reputation, CV volume, and personal relationships; networking and in-person interactions can advantage those 'in the room' and perpetuate Matthew Effect biases toward established investigators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit guidance on whether and how to consider applicant reputation; consider blinding/anonymisation where feasible; minimise informal social interactions that may bias deliberations; and actively recruit diverse reviewers and applicants to mitigate reputation-driven advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the Chair in ensuring transparency and rigour
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chair was described as essential for guiding discussion, establishing calibration (floor/ceiling), managing conflicts, interceding on inappropriate rationale (eg, funding due to repeated resubmission), and minimising bias during consensus meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select Chairs with strong facilitation and interpersonal skills in addition to scientific credibility; provide Chairs with targeted training (conflict management, calibration techniques, bias mitigation) and clear mandates to manage scoring consistency and enforce process rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer time constraints and stretched resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer roles are largely volunteer and reviewers report heavy competing academic and personal commitments, limiting time for careful review and for undertaking training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders and institutions should consider measures to reduce reviewer burden (eg, compensated time, workload recognition, streamlined processes), protect time for peer review duties, and design review tasks cognizant of reviewers' capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration (score calibration talk and setting common standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Committees benefit from explicit calibration: discussing and agreeing what constitutes example scores (eg, what is a 3.5 vs 4.1) so members reach 'common ground' and apply the scale more consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Chair-led calibration at the start of meetings (identify exemplar top and bottom grants), encourage explicit verbal description matching numeric scores, and document calibration anchors to reduce intra- and inter-panel variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the full scoring range and clear messaging in scores/comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants noted reluctance to use the extremes of the scale (few very low scores) and frustration with tightly clustered mid-range scores (eg, 3.5 vs 3.6) that obscure funding/non-funding signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage appropriate use of the full scale so consensus scores and written feedback clearly indicate fundable versus non-fundable status; ensure written feedback aligns with the numeric score to send 'a clear message' to applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranking versus rating as allocation approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Rating is an absolute judgement on an ordinal scale (eg, poor to excellent) while ranking orders applications relative to one another. Participants reported debate about merits of each; the study found ranking to be more reliable and less susceptible to reviewer differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider adopting ranking (relative judgement) or hybrid approaches for allocating funds, or ensure comprehensive training and calibration if retaining rating; evaluate empirically which approach yields more reproducible funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlining criteria for eliminating non-competitive applications
rubrics_metrics.description: CIHR's streamlining process excludes applications from discussion if: (1) the reviewers' average places the application in the bottom 60% of the committee's pool, (2) at least one reviewer has identified it as non-competitive, and (3) no committee member objects to streamlining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply clear, pre-specified streamlining rules to conserve committee time for competitive applications; ensure transparency about these criteria and allow procedures for objections to prevent inappropriate exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent and transparent handling of resubmissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants observed inconsistent treatment of resubmitted applications and some reviewers attempted to push repeated resubmissions over the funding line for reasons unrelated to current proposal quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit guidance on how to review resubmissions (eg, evaluate on current merits, note prior history without letting it dictate funding), and empower Chairs to intercede when resubmission history is used improperly as a rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinding/double anonymisation to reduce identity-based bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Including applicants' CVs with applications can introduce bias favoring well-known investigators; evidence from journal peer review suggests double-blind review reduces bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider feasibility of blinding applicants' identities and affiliations in grant review; at minimum, provide explicit policy on whether applicant reputation should be considered and under which circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit informal social interactions that may introduce bias
rubrics_metrics.description: In-person social moments (eg, dinners, side conversations) were reported to create networking benefits but also to influence deliberations and bias scores toward those present or well-connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit or formalise out-of-meeting interactions during active review periods; create alternative community-building opportunities (training events) that do not coincide with adjudication; adopt rules similar to jury sequester practices to reduce off-record influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of partial lottery/random allocation for the meritorious middle
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants and cited literature suggested that when many applications are plausibly fundable but funds are limited, a partial lottery (random allocation after thresholding) can be fairer, more efficient, and more diverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider implementing a partial lottery for applications above a quality threshold to reduce time spent splitting hairs, investigate acceptability among stakeholders, and monitor effects on fairness and diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and assignment of reviewers to ensure expertise and diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: CIHR recruits reviewers from its College and other sources and assigns up to 20-member committees; the selection and assignment of qualified reviewers influences review quality and equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure reviewer pools and committee composition represent disciplinary breadth and under-represented regions/groups; match reviewer expertise to applications carefully and document assignment rationale to improve fairness and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and clarity of feedback to applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants receive the final rating, written feedback summarising committee discussion, and individual reviewer comments, but there is no interview or rebuttal during selection; participants stressed feedback should clearly reflect funding intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure written feedback is aligned with scores, clearly communicates fundability and reasons, and consider structured opportunities (eg, two-page Response to Previous Reviews on resubmission) while maintaining finality of committee decisions during the round.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity, diversity and inclusion (EDI) considerations in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Minoritised and early-career researchers may be disadvantaged (eg, Matthew Effect, limited networking), and participants urged attention to EDI practices to improve transparency and rigour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate EDI practices into reviewer recruitment, training, anonymisation policies, and monitoring; research and track impacts of procedural changes on diversity and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus rating procedure and final rating constraints (CIHR practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: CIHR process: three reviewers provide initial ratings; at committee meeting the three reviewers aim for a consensus rating (often the mean); once announced, all committee members give a final rating within ±0.5 of the consensus rating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about consensus and final rating rules, monitor whether the ±0.5 constraint promotes or suppresses honest independent judgement, and consider whether alternative aggregation/statistical compensation (eg, z-score normalization) could address systematic reviewer differences.
